A company claiming to be headquartered in Vietnam, "Fun Coffee", has been accused of operating a virtual currency investment scam under the guise of investing in a coffee business. Police arrested six people yesterday, with the amount involved reaching HK$94 million. Several victims stated at a press conference today (the 5th) that they initially only earned a few hundred dollars by filming videos after being introduced by friends, before being persuaded to invest in "doing tasks". One victim said they had initially suspected it might be a scam, but the company held numerous events, including an "exchange" trip to Singapore and marathons with free entry for "members", which led them to believe the company was listed and they gradually let down their guard after investing large sums. Legislative Council member Ng Kit-chong said he had received求助 from about 50 victims and hoped law enforcement agencies would take swift action to freeze the relevant assets.

Several victims met the press today (the 5th) arranged by Legislative Council member Ng Kit-chong. They said they were initially introduced to the "work" by friends, and could earn $400 by filming a few minutes of video. Afterwards, they were gradually persuaded step by step to download a mobile app and deposit stablecoin USDT to "do tasks" in exchange for high returns. A "upline-downline" mechanism was also set up, offering rewards for introducing others to become "members".

The Fun Coffee mobile app offers various investment products, showing that the longer the funds are kept, the higher the return, with each user assigned a "quota". One product named "Smart Coffee Beverage Delivery Robot" showed a total interest rate of 296.4%. A victim explained that if a user deposited HK$160,000, after 390 days they could withdraw over HK$474,000, plus nearly HK$150,000 in "tier bonus returns".

700-person "team" chain: Victim says boss claimed they were benefiting and guaranteed profits

Under the upline-downline "human chain" mechanism, Victim A, Ms A, claimed her "team" had as many as 700 people, but she frankly said she did not understand investing and did not consider Fun Coffee an investment project. She quoted the company "boss" telling her that the company intended to go public within three years and had already received many orders: "The boss said the company has plenty of money, but to develop the brand it needs more people to know about it, so us in the first batch are very fortunate, these tasks benefit us and profits are guaranteed." She took it at face value, and even pooled money with others to purchase task packages. She did see returns initially, but ultimately 50 people in her team became victims unable to withdraw funds, with total losses estimated at HK$14 million.

Ms A's "downline" Sandy estimated losses of about HK$900,000. She said the company held events every two to three months, including dinners, exchange sessions, and marathons. She said that in April this year, after being persuaded, she invested over HK$600,000 and gained the opportunity to attend a "Summit Exchange" in Singapore. Sandy said the other party claimed at the time that the HK$600,000-plus, after being kept for seven months, could be withdrawn with HK$1.4 million in profit. After returning to Hong Kong, there were continuous "meetings", with some claiming they would expand into the Mainland market.

Told "investing in coffee" was like a bank fixed deposit: Victim took out loans to increase investment

Mr Wong also completed filming tasks after being introduced by a friend, and a few months later downloaded the mobile app to start "investing in coffee". The other party said it was "like a bank fixed deposit, upon maturity you safely get back your principal and interest". He initially earned returns smoothly, so he gradually increased his "investment" amount, ultimately pouring all his savings of over HK$400,000 into it. Later, after being persuaded over the phone by a self-proclaimed company executive "Boss Cheung", he took out two loans totalling HK$190,000 to increase his "investment". However, after his investment matured last month, the withdrawal channel showed as closed, leaving about HK$600,000 irretrievable.

A victim who did not wish to be named said they had initially suspected it was a scam, but noted the company held numerous events, including marathons with free entry for members: "Many people said if they wanted to scam people, spending millions on a marathon wouldn't make sense." "(A friend said) If the company scams you, when would they ever make back this kind of money?" This made them let down their guard.

Lawmaker Ng Kit-chong calls for swift freezing of related assets

After the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) issued a warning on its website last month, listing the Fun Coffee project as a suspicious investment product, many people became unable to withdraw funds and all the "bosses" could no longer be contacted. Hong Kong Police and Macau Judicial Police conducted a joint operation yesterday. Hong Kong Police said they had received about 225 reports, involving approximately HK$94 million, and six people arrested have been released on bail; Macau Judicial Police arrested two people, involving 9 cases totalling about 3.6 million Macanese patacas.

Legislative Council member Ng Kit-chong urged authorities to take swift action to freeze the relevant assets. He also suggested improving mechanisms so that when law enforcement agencies detect suspicious transactions on a platform, they can freeze cryptocurrency assets at the same time as issuing warnings, to increase victims' chances of recovering scammed funds and prevent fraudsters from absconding with the money in time.

Artist Yuen Siu-cheung was reportedly the host of a Fun Coffee marathon event last December. He responded yesterday (the 4th) on social media, stating that the event was "an employee marathon race for a brand", and that the hosting script did not involve product introductions or promotions for the company. After completing the day's work, he did not collaborate with or contact the brand again. Police said yesterday that during the investigation they would contact victims and relevant parties to determine the mastermind of the scam and the roles played.
